batch_notes: (1) Recurring shape the rubric does not name: 'generator-side model' -- the generator builds a structured value, renders it to text with a test-written writer, and the assertion is parse(text) == the value's expected form (rust/apt-sources *_are_read_as_the_model_says and its 11 pins, go/yaml TestHegelGeneratedDocumentsLoadToTheTreeTheyWereWrittenFrom). The expected value is known by construction, not by a substantive alternative computation, so I filed these as spec-postcondition per the rubric text, but the READMEs call it a 'model' and other classifiers may say model-oracle; a ruling would help consistency. (2) 'f(x) == x by value' preservation properties (bigdecimal normalized_preserves_value, rounding_to_larger_scale_is_exact) sit between algebraic-law 'identity' and spec-postcondition; filed spec-postcondition. Small spec-transcribed validity predicates deciding acceptance (bech32 prop_segwit_encode_validity_matches_spec, prop_encode_enforces_code_length_limit) filed spec-postcondition rather than model-oracle. (3) rust/apt-sources: every one of its 11 bugs is recorded against a dedicated narrowed property (tagged pin here), while the general properties gate around them (e.g. legacy_display_round_trips skips pdiffs for apt-sources/5). Direct attribution therefore credits the pins, and the target's bug rate without pin-tagged properties will be zero even though the general properties almost certainly found the bugs first. (4) go/yaml: all 15 bugs are pinned by plain Go example tests; the README's 'Generator avoidances' section states which generator restriction corresponds to each pin, which supports inferred attribution to the general properties but only names a specific property for yaml/10, /11, /14. Its properties have no doc comments (the README carries the descriptions). (5) Quality: nothing broken; go/yaml and rust/apt-sources are the notable targets (three external YAML readers incl. a PyYAML child process; APT itself and python-apt as oracles).
